[[Category:Large language model]]

The '''data wall''' describes the regime in which the supply of high-quality human-written text fit for [[large language model (LLM)]] training is exhausted.<ref>{{#cite:Q3181}}</ref>

== Increasing demand ==

Let $D_{\max}$ be the stock of available human-written tokens and $C$ the training compute. The [[Chinchilla prescription]] allocates to token in a fixed compute budget

$$
D_{\text{opt}}(C)\propto C^{\alpha_{|\theta|}/(\alpha_{|\theta|}+\alpha_D)},
$$

According to [[Source:Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Conference paper)|name-author]], $\alpha_{|\theta|} \approx \alpha_D$, hence

$$
D \propto C^\frac{1}{2},
$$

i.e., when the compute budget grows by 4 fold, the optimal dataset size grows by about 2.

<ref>{{#cite:Q3164}}</ref>

== Timing ==
[[File:LLM training data bottleneck.png|thumbnail|300px]]
The effective stock of quality-filtered, deduplicated publicly available human-written text is estimated to be around

$$
D_{\max}\approx 3\times10^{14}\ \text{tokens},
$$

According to estimates of [[Source:Will we run out of data? Limits of LLM scaling based on human-generated data (Conference paper)|name-author]], if current trends continue, the stock would be depleted between 2026 and 2032.

<ref>{{#cite:Q3181}}</ref>

== Repetition ==

Repeating the tokens already in hand is a partial substitute. Writing $R=D/D_{\max}$ for the number of epochs, the value of repeated data saturates,

$$
D_{\text{eff}}=D_{\max}\left(1+R^{\ast}\left(1-e^{-R/R^{\ast}}\right)\right),
$$

where $R^{\ast}$ is a fitted decay constant. Two consequences follow: up to roughly 4 epochs, repeated data costs almost nothing in loss relative to unique data, and, because $D_{\text{eff}}\to D_{\max}(1+R^{\ast})$ as $R\to\infty$, no amount of repetition substitutes for more unique text.<ref>{{#cite:Q3174}}</ref>
